subject: chemistry_2
question_text: What is a biodegradable polymer? Give two examples.

verification.note: Unit 12 (Polymers), printed as VSAQ 7 on book p.95. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board scheme, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Source: the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", printed chapter 9 (POLYMERS), book pp.95-98 (PDF pp.34-37), which is unit 12 in this bank. The chapter is VSAQ-only: it prints 24 Very Short Answer Questions and has no Short Answer and no Long Answer section at all, and no PROBLEMS. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK WORDING AND EXAMPLES: the printed answer is "A polymer which is decomposed by the action of a microorganisms are called bio-degradable polymer", with examples PHBV and Polylactic acid. The grammar is broken and is rewritten; the chemistry is correct and is kept. NCERT gives the pair PHBV and nylon-2-nylon-6, so this card names all three and a student is not caught out by either wording. GAP: the book names polylactic acid but never its monomer, which is lactic acid, 2-hydroxypropanoic acid; it is supplied here. Nylon-2-nylon-6 appears in the same chapter at VSAQ 14, but the book never says there that it is biodegradable.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: A biodegradable polymer is one that is
broken down in the environment by
micro-organisms, or by hydrolysis of the
links in its own chain, into simple
products such as CO₂ and H₂O.
Most of them are polyesters or
steps.why: The ester and amide links in these polymers are the same links enzymes break in fats and proteins, so soil organisms can break them too. A chain of plain C–C bonds, as in polythene, has no such link, which is why ordinary plastics last.
common_mistakes: Writing that a biodegradable polymer dissolves in water. It is broken down by micro-organisms or by hydrolysis of its links.
Giving polythene or PVC as an example. Their chains have only C–C bonds, so nothing can hydrolyse them.
steps.memory_tip: Ester and amide links can be broken by living things; plain C–C chains cannot.
steps.margin_note: The words decomposed by micro-organisms are the mark. Naming the products is a bonus.

steps.label: Two examples with their monomers
lines: Polylactic acid, made from lactic acid,
steps.why: PHBV and polylactic acid are built from hydroxy acids that living cells already make, and nylon-2–nylon-6 has the same amide links as protein. In every case soil organisms can hydrolyse the ester or amide links. Naming the monomers is what shows the example was understood rather than remembered.
common_mistakes: Writing the name PHBV without naming its monomers. The two hydroxy acids are why it breaks down.
Giving only one example. The question asks for two.
steps.memory_tip: Both standard examples have links that living things can hydrolyse: ester links in PHBV, amide links in nylon-2–nylon-6.
steps.margin_note: Two names finish this mark. The monomers are one extra line and are worth writing.

insider_note: The book prints PHBV and polylactic acid, while NCERT prints PHBV and nylon-2–nylon-6. All three are correct, so write PHBV and then either of the other two.
